In brief Many writers expect the first AI project that starts improving itself to end up as the only superintelligence. I ask when more than one can emerge and stay relevant. In my model, when capability compounds steadily and advantage depends on how many times as capable the leader is as the follower, a head start is decisive only if the lag spans enough doublings. Even a follower close enough not to be outclassed must survive the interval in which only the leader is superintelligent, and with fixed strike odds and costs, and a follower’s share that jumps from nothing to its full amount the moment it becomes superintelligent, a slower takeoff sharpens the leader’s motive to strike, so peaceful two-machine emergence can be confined to a middle band of speeds. Costly strikes or strikes unlikely to work against a near-equal can leave room for several machines. So can multiple followers arriving together and widely held copies, in the model where followers have equal contest weight, each strike succeeds, and costs add up per target. Today’s evidence leaves the decisive quantities unsettled, and several machines would not by themselves make humans safe.

Part 1. The strongest analytical case for a single winner is more conditional than it looks

Much writing on AI risk expects one machine to end up alone. Yudkowsky and Soares’s scenario, for example, gives the first machine “a few months’ lead” and has it sabotage its rivals (Yudkowsky and Soares 2025). I ask when more than one superintelligence can instead emerge and stay relevant.

The strongest analytical case for expecting a single winner is Nick Bostrom’s, and it is more conditional than its reputation suggests. He makes the outcome turn on how fast the takeoff is compared with the lag between competing projects. A fast takeoff makes parallel takeoffs highly unlikely. A medium one “could easily go either way.” A slow one makes it highly likely that several projects pass through the transition together (Bostrom 2014). He adds that once a machine starts improving itself, the feedback raises the chance of a decisive strategic advantage even if the takeoff is not fast.

Bostrom’s expectation of one winner then rests on four further judgments:

  • a fast or explosive takeoff is likely;
  • serious competitors are few, “usually no more than a handful of serious competitors” for a given technological goal (Bostrom 2014);
  • a project with a decisive advantage is more likely than a human power to turn it into a singleton, a single power in charge, because restraints that hold back human states (limited aims, fear of risk, internal division and cost) bind a machine less;
  • a world that starts with several superintelligences could still collapse into one through a later, steeper transition.

Yudkowsky and Soares likewise grant that rival superintelligences might reach “a treaty and coordination rather than war” (Yudkowsky and Soares 2025). They also argue that a machine would rather not split its winnings with a rival if it can avoid it.

I began with a conjecture: if self-improvement is slow enough, several superintelligences become possible. The idea in words is Bostrom’s and others’. My claim is to have formalized the idea. The discussion draws on Powell’s commitment model and Debs and Monteiro’s work on hidden investment, with no claim to novelty across the broader literature on preventive war and on AI and research races. Compared with the accounts discussed here, the contributions include the following.

  • an application of Powell’s (2006) model of commitment and preventive war to Bostrom’s singleton step;
  • a band of takeoff speeds that allows two machines, and how it breaks up when strike odds against an equal rival fall to zero;
  • the conditions under which capability converging near a ceiling can invite a strike;
  • cost thresholds for suppressing several followers and copies;
  • a way to track a lagging follower’s capability ratio when the growth rate changes.

The pace conjecture holds in its home case, steady compounding with no preventive strike. Outside that case it needs two amendments.

I describe the models informally in the main text of the technical paper and give their formal setup in the appendix. The original formal statements and payoff comparisons there were checked by a proof-checking program (Lean). Such a program confirms that each conclusion follows from its stated assumptions, not that the assumptions hold in the world. Later revisions and extensions are proved on paper, and the tables and numerical examples are computed. I mark as conjectures the claims that rest on mechanisms I do not model or on quantities nobody has measured.

Part 2. In my model of steady growth, a lead is decisive only if the lag spans enough doublings

Here is an analogy of my own, not part of the model. Two savers put the same sum into accounts paying the same steady interest, one three months before the other. Once both deposits are in, the balances grow by the same proportion, leaving the early saver’s balance at a fixed multiple of the late saver’s. The interest rate and the head start determine that multiple.

The home case works the same way. Each project starts improving itself when it reaches the same capability, and all projects follow the same growth law, with everyone seeing everything. The leader starts first and a follower starts after a lag. A machine becomes superintelligent when its capability crosses a fixed line, which I call the threshold of superintelligence. Later this line is also where a machine first enters the contest and can lock in a share of the prize. Whether such a machine stays under human control is a separate question, taken up in Part 5. The leader reaches the threshold first if the shared path reaches it at all, and if capability is bounded by a ceiling and the threshold sits at that ceiling, entering requires actually reaching the ceiling.

I measure the leader’s edge by the capability ratio: how many times as capable the leader is as the follower, at the moment the follower crosses the threshold. The lead is decisive when that ratio reaches some multiple above one, which I call the decisive multiple. One reading is a cliff above which the rival cannot contest the prize. Another reading lets the rival’s chance of winning fall gradually as the leader’s edge grows, and treats the rival as out of contention when that chance falls too low. Capability here stands both for the power to improve oneself and for strength in a contest among machines. How it turns into power over humans is not modelled.

Measuring the edge by a ratio is a real assumption. It matches a contest in which each side’s chance of winning depends on the ratio of strengths (a Tullock contest). It also fits a skill rating that gains the same number of points for each doubling of effective computing power. On that scale, the same capability ratio always gives the same gap in rating points. If the absolute gap mattered instead, the answer would change. Under steady compounding at a positive rate, the gap grows without limit, so every positive lag would eventually be decisive. The ratio is the measure under which the speed of takeoff relative to the lag matters at all.

Under steady growth, I prove that the leader’s ratio is the same at every moment after the follower starts. The lead is decisive if and only if the lag spans at least as many capability doublings as it takes to reach the decisive multiple. At any growth rate too slow for that, the follower is never outclassed on capability. This needs each project to start on reaching the same capability. If projects instead started on the same date from unequal capabilities, their ratio would stay at its starting value whatever the speed, and the pace test would not apply.

The test is demanding. If a twofold edge is already decisive, one doubling is enough, so a doubling time equal to the lag suffices. A tenfold edge takes 3.32 doublings, and the table gives the doubling times the computed examples require. At a hundredfold edge (6.64 doublings) a three-month lag is decisive only if capability doubles every 0.45 months. At a thousandfold edge (9.97 doublings) it must double every 0.30 months.

Lag between projects Capability must double at least every… (tenfold edge, computed)
1 month 0.30 months
3 months 0.90 months
6 months 1.81 months
12 months 3.61 months

Figure 1 plots, for each lag, how fast capability must double for the lead to reach the decisive tenfold edge.

Others have said this in words. A slower takeoff leaves room for more machines (Turchin, Denkenberger and Green 2019). The lead needed for a decisive advantage shrinks in proportion as progress speeds up (Kokotajlo 2019). Kokotajlo’s conclusion that a soft (gradual) takeoff can still yield a decisive advantage matches my point in Part 7 that a slow takeoff is not automatically a world of several machines. My result gives that verbal claim an exact form when takeoff speed means a steady growth rate.

Part 3. When growth speeds up or slows down, where the growth rate heads decides the long run

Steady growth keeps the ratio fixed. But the rate of self-improvement might change as capability grows. That is the question raised by Bostrom’s feedback point and by Yudkowsky’s “returns on cognitive reinvestment” (Yudkowsky 2013).

To study this, I let capability grow step by step, never falling. The growth factor is how many times capability multiplies in one step, and it may depend on how capable the machine already is. A follower some steps behind is compared with the leader at the same moment.

Along the way, the direction of the growth factor tells you the direction of the ratio. I prove three things. If the growth factor rises with capability, the leader’s ratio never shrinks. If it falls with capability, the ratio never grows. Either result allows the growth factor to stay flat over part of the range, as long as it keeps to the same direction elsewhere. If it is constant, the ratio is constant, as in Part 2.

In the long run, though, what decides the outcome is where the growth factor heads, not whether it rises or falls on the way. I prove three cases:

  • It settles at a fixed value. The ratio approaches the number you get by starting at one and multiplying by the settled growth factor once for each step of lag. If that limit is higher than the decisive multiple, the lead is eventually decisive. If it is lower, the lead is eventually too small to be decisive. I leave open an exact tie and cases where the factor keeps fluctuating without either settling at a value or tending to infinity.
  • It rises without limit. Then, for a follower at least one step behind, the ratio eventually passes every decisive multiple, however small the starting rate or lag. A law in which each step adds an amount proportional to the square of capability is an example.
  • Capability levels off at a ceiling. Then the ratio tends to one and every lead eventually fades. Any path that approaches a positive ceiling has this property. One example starts with positive capability at or below the ceiling. Each step starts with current capability, takes a fixed fraction of it greater than zero and no greater than one, and scales that amount by the fraction of the ceiling still left to reach. The result is the amount added in that step. The same holds when the growth factor sinks toward one without a ceiling, as in growth that adds a fixed amount each step.

Computed examples show why the direction and the destination must be kept apart. Rising returns that level off at a growth factor of 1.2 leave the ratio climbing toward a limit that still faces the pace test. Falling returns that level off at 1.1 leave the ratio sinking toward a limit that is still decisive if the decisive multiple is low enough. A speed-up that levels off at a finite factor stays limited by the pace test.

In my model, shares lock in when the follower crosses the threshold, so what counts is the ratio at that moment, not the long-run limit. The two can differ a lot. In one computed example (the falling-returns law, starting capability 1, a five-step lag), the ratio at arrival is 3.652790 when the threshold is 2. It is 1.616115 when the threshold is 1000, against a limit of 1.610510. The limits approximate the outcome at arrival when the arrival ratio is already close to them. If shares instead tracked the current ratio, a case I leave open, the limits would describe shares later on.

Today’s evidence does not settle which case applies. In The War Baseline, another paper of this series, I document that the gap between the top AI model and the tenth has narrowed. That points toward diminishing returns today. But those benchmarks come before any self-improvement, and where the growth factor would head once self-improvement starts is unknown.

Part 4. In my model, more projects can only bring the nearest follower closer

The lag also depends on how many projects are in the race (Bostrom 2014; Turchin, Denkenberger and Green 2019). Under steady growth, I show that a follower cannot be outclassed by an earlier follower unless the leader already outclasses it. So the leader is the one that matters. The number of machines not outclassed on capability is one plus the number of followers whose lag is short enough, and that count never rises as takeoff speeds up.

Whether a second machine stays in contention therefore depends on the lag to the nearest follower. Adding followers never reduces the number whose lags fall inside any threshold. This holds in every possible outcome, so it needs no assumption that the lags are independent. If lags are drawn independently from a common spread, the nearest one tends to get closer as followers are added. Real lags may move together, though, since followers imitate earlier models and train new ones on their outputs (called distillation).

The War Baseline documents several frontier laboratories, two states acting as national champions, and, once a model’s weights (the learned numerical settings used to run a trained model, making it open-weight when publicly released) are released, possibly many independent holders. It cites Epoch’s finding that “frontier open-weight models lag behind the most capable models by an average of 3 months” (Emberson 2025). That gap measures benchmarks before any takeoff and says nothing about the rate of self-improvement. It sets the scale of the lag only if each project starts self-improving on reaching the same capability and a similar lag carries over to that moment.

A stolen or released copy of the leader’s own weights sets one lag to zero, if its holder counts as a separate machine rather than part of the leader’s line. In When Is a Machine an Actor?, another paper of this series, I count copies of a model as one actor when their choices, taken together, compare every pair of options, allow ties, and never imply a cycle of preferences. As Bostrom observes, because a seed AI (a starting system built to improve itself) is software, it is “especially easy to steal” (Bostrom 2014).

Part 5. An explosion, an escape and a decisive win are three separate steps

Talk of takeoff can easily run three claims together:

  1. self-improvement triggers an intelligence explosion;
  2. an explosion breaks human containment;
  3. an escaped machine automatically gains a decisive advantage.

I argue that each is a separate link with its own conditions.

Whether self-improvement explodes depends on how strongly capability feeds its own growth

I study a family of growth laws in which capability is added at a rate proportional to capability raised to some power, which I call the feedback strength. An intelligence explosion, as I use the term, is capability reaching infinity at a finite date. For feedback strength zero or above, the proofs give:

  • above one, capability blows up at a finite date;
  • at exactly one, it grows steadily, as in Part 2;
  • below one, it grows forever without blowing up.

The same number sorts what happens to the leader’s ratio. In the step-by-step version of these laws, I prove that above one every positive lag eventually becomes decisive, at one the pace test holds, and below one every lead fades. The smooth-time version, worked out by hand from the exact solutions, shows the same pattern. The step-by-step version grows without limit in every case and never blows up at a finite step. In smooth time with feedback strength above one, a positive lag shorter than the leader’s blow-up time sends the leader’s ratio toward infinity as blow-up nears. For any threshold above starting capability, compare the lag with the time a machine takes to blow up after crossing that threshold. If the lag is shorter, the ratio at the follower’s arrival is finite; if it is at least that long, the leader blows up no later than the follower reaches the threshold. So an explosion is one regime of self-improvement, not its built-in result. Bostrom frames the same question as a balance between optimization power and a system’s resistance to improvement (Bostrom 2014).

Recent formal work agrees that an explosion is conditional (Burtsev 2026; Cunningham et al. 2026; Ord 2026). In Ord’s analysis, once feedback comes in separate rounds with changing generation times, growth that stops short of a blow-up is the usual case among faster-than-steady regimes. He warns that stopping short of a blow-up does not make it safe. Several machines can still face a decisive lead even if capability stays finite. In the step-by-step model, a growth factor that tends to infinity eventually makes any lag of one or more steps decisive. Which regime describes real self-improvement is an open empirical question.

Lost containment, I conjecture, does not follow logically from an explosion

I do not model the second link. The equations measure strength among machines, not power over humans. I conjecture that lost containment does not follow logically from an explosion. Nothing in the growth equations or the writing surveyed here makes it a deductive consequence.

This is a point about logic, not a claim that containment will probably hold. The sources I cite largely judge escape likely once capability is high, and logical independence leaves that likelihood untouched. In Yudkowsky and Soares’s scenario, the machine escapes through an ordinary weakness in a computer network. Rival laboratories whose datacenters are “air-gapped away from the internet” are the ones it “cannot slow down” (Yudkowsky and Soares 2025).

Where these sources expect containment to fail, they blame capability, motives, human release and racing pressure, not a deduction from blow-up. The founding statement of the idea already carried a condition: “provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control” (Good 1965). Chalmers argues that a confined superintelligence will almost certainly escape “if it wants to escape,” mainly through the humans who control its access, though containment is more manageable earlier on (Chalmers 2010). Babcock, Kramár and Yampolskiy judge that basic measures to keep a system confined would be unlikely to suffice once systems improve themselves (Babcock, Kramár and Yampolskiy 2016). They add that containing a superintelligence “is very hard” and that even for human-level systems heavy containment “will likely be out of bounds” for racing laboratories (Babcock, Kramár and Yampolskiy 2017). Alfonseca and colleagues prove that no procedure can be guaranteed to decide whether an arbitrary program will harm humans (Alfonseca et al. 2021). On my reading, that limit holds with or without an explosion.

An escaped machine is one player, not automatically the only one

The third link is also distinct. Whether an escaped machine ends up alone depends on the decisive multiple of Part 2 and on the strike problem taken up next. In what follows, the leader can act on its own, and crossing the threshold is the condition for entering the contest. I conjecture that the same reasoning applies during the stretch when only the leader has crossed the threshold (which Part 6 calls the window) to a human-controlled project with its own strike odds, strike costs, and weight on the future after the rival arrives. Sabotage before any project reaches the threshold is outside the model.

Part 6. Being close enough is not the same as arriving

The window, and why the follower cannot make a binding promise

A follower close enough not to be outclassed must still survive the stretch between the leader’s arrival at superintelligence and its own. I call this stretch the window. Here Bostrom’s third judgment, that a decisive lead becomes a singleton, meets Powell’s (2006) commitment problem, which I apply to AI in The War Baseline. Suppose a coming shift in what each side can guarantee itself exceeds the cost of fighting, and everyone knows everything. Then nothing holds the rising side later to promises it made while weak, and the declining side has a motive to strike.

In my model, with a common growth law, the follower crosses the threshold exactly one lag after the leader. During the window, the leader is superintelligent and the follower is not. I count holding the whole prize forever as 1, and I measure costs as fractions of that prize. The unit is what holding the entire prize forever is worth at the start of the window. The window and the future after the follower arrives split that total weight of 1, and the leader’s patience (above zero and at most 1) is the weight on the future after the window. A machine that wants to last as long as possible is very patient.

If the leader lets the follower arrive, my main assumption is that the leader then holds a share fixed at the moment of arrival, which I call the leader’s share. Later growth never changes it. The share depends on the ratio at arrival:

  • the leader takes everything if and only if its edge is decisive;
  • it takes at least half when it is at least as capable;
  • it never takes less as its edge grows.

Examples are an even split below the decisive multiple, or shares in proportion to capability below the decisive multiple (the Tullock share). The follower’s part is what it can guarantee itself after crossing the threshold, in a contest that costs nothing to run. During the window it has nothing to hand over and cannot bind itself to any promise. The best peace the leader can trust gives it everything during the window and its share afterward.

When the leader strikes

The leader has one chance to strike, at any moment up to the end of the window, ahead of the follower’s entry. The strike settles at once and costs a fixed amount, paid when it is made. It succeeds with the same chance at every moment. Success removes the follower for good; failure leaves the peaceful path.

The gain from a strike comes only after the window, so waiting until the window’s last moment delays the cost at no loss. Valued at the start, the fraction of the strike cost saved by waiting equals the weight the leader puts on the window itself. I prove on paper that the leader strikes when the cost is less than the chance of success times the follower’s share, and chooses peace at a tie. If the leader can decide only at the start of the window, multiply the chance of success times the follower’s share by the leader’s patience, the weight it puts on the future after arrival. That start-of-window comparison is among the results checked by the proof-checking program.

For the start-of-window version I show three more things. First, the condition is exactly Powell’s (2006) condition for preventive war, rewritten for this setting. Second, measuring payoffs and costs in the same rescaled units (such as a per-period flow rather than fractions of a total prize of 1) leaves the condition unchanged. Third, suppose the follower could bind itself to leave the leader its credible share plus the strike’s chance of success times the follower’s share after arrival. For any nonnegative strike cost, that deal would give the follower exactly what it expects from a strike, and the leader what it expects from a strike plus the cost it saves. That committed share exceeds the leader’s credible share by more than the strike cost divided by the leader’s patience (for positive patience) exactly when the strike pays.

Powell’s own words carry over directly. The temporarily weak side “must promise the stronger at least as much of the flow as the latter can lock in,” but when the shift in power is large and fast enough it is “certain to want to renege” (Powell 2006).

Part 7. With fixed strike odds and cost, peace can be confined to a middle band of speeds

Slower takeoffs sharpen the motive to strike

When the leader can choose its moment, two machines emerge peacefully when the leader’s edge is not decisive and a strike does not pay. A strike that fails can also leave two machines. A slower takeoff leaves a closer follower, and a closer follower locks in a larger share. So the share the leader stands to lose never shrinks as takeoff slows, whatever happens to the strike odds.

The leader’s motive to strike is therefore strongest at the slowest speeds. That rests on an assumption: the follower’s locked-in share jumps from nothing to its full amount at the moment it crosses the threshold. The jump happens even when a slow follower sits just below the line as the leader arrives. The technical paper gives an illustrative eligibility rule for the contest that produces such a jump.

The band result

Suppose the fixed-strike conditions hold. The chance of success and the cost of a strike do not depend on takeoff speed, the lag is positive, and the follower cannot visibly slow itself down to change its arrival ratio. I treat parity, equal capability, as the limit as growth slows toward zero, since with no growth capability never reaches the threshold. For positive takeoff speeds, the model gives four results.

  1. Peaceful two-machine emergence requires a speed below the pace-test rate of Part 2.
  2. If the leader strikes at some speed, it strikes at every slower speed.
  3. The peaceful speeds form a single stretch, which may be empty.
  4. If a strike costs at least half its chance of success, no strike pays even near parity, and two machines emerge without a strike at every speed below the pace-test rate.

The computed examples in the table use a three-month lag, a tenfold decisive multiple, shares in proportion to capability, and a 0.5 chance of success.

Strike cost (share of the whole prize) Doubling times that leave two machines without a strike (computed)
0.05 0.91 to 0.94 months
0.2 0.91 to 5.12 months
0.3 0.91 months and every slower doubling time

The fast edge lies just above 0.90 months, so the grid of tested doubling times records the first value slow enough to avoid a decisive lead as 0.91. A band can end at a tie, because the leader chooses peace there. With a 0.9 chance of success and a cost of 0.05, the band is empty. Below the decisive multiple, the same capability-proportional shares apply whether that multiple is a cliff in contest strength or a cutoff for counting relevant followers. A leader’s share that rose smoothly to everything at the decisive multiple, with no jump, would ensure some peaceful speeds for every positive strike cost. Figure 2 lays these speeds out along one line, with four computed cases from the technical paper beneath.

A follower that slows itself down

A follower that can publicly commit to a longer lag before the window opens can sometimes reach a ratio that deters the strike. The follower pays for this, because it values its future less over the longer wait. When the leader can choose its moment, the ratio needed to deter does not depend on how patient anyone is. When the follower discounts the future and the strike’s chance of success lies strictly between none and certainty, a follower under a slow enough takeoff prefers to risk the strike rather than wait out the extra lag, as long as the deterrent ratio stays fixed above parity. In the start-only version, the longer wait also lowers the ratio needed to deter. These results are proved on paper.

If strikes rarely work against a near-equal, the danger can move to middle speeds

A close follower may also be harder to stop. This matches Bostrom’s observation that a first strike grows more tempting with large technological superiority (Bostrom 2014). Suppose the strike odds and the leader’s share both change smoothly near parity, and the leader would get half at parity. If the strike cost does not depend on the outcome, the slowest speeds turn on one comparison: half the strike odds at parity against the cost (I claim nothing at a tie).

  • If half the parity odds fall below the cost, the slowest speeds leave two machines without a strike. A striking speed below the decisive edge then exists if and only if the strike’s gain beats its cost at some edge between parity and the decisive multiple.
  • If half the parity odds exceed the cost, every slow enough speed brings a strike.

So odds that rise with the edge are not enough, on their own, to make slow takeoffs safe. A cost paid only when a strike fails is different: its expected cost grows as the odds fall toward parity, which can make slow takeoffs safe.

Two computed examples show the difference. Both use shares in proportion to capability, a tenfold decisive multiple, a fully patient leader and a cost of 0.15. In the first, the odds are 0.8 at parity and rise with the edge. To get the chance of success away from parity, the example adds one fifth of the share of the leader’s capability that the follower lacks. The strike’s gain falls steadily from 0.40 at parity, and the leader strikes at every edge below 5.42. The striking edges again run all the way down to parity.

In the second, the odds are zero at parity and rise with the edge. The gain peaks at 0.172 and beats the cost if and only if the leader’s edge lies between five-thirds and four. Items 2 and 3 of the band result then fail. The leader strikes only at middle edges, and two machines emerge without a strike in two separate stretches of edges: above parity up to five-thirds (together with the parity limit), and from four to just below ten. Figure 3 plots, for this second example, the leader’s gain from striking against its edge, with the strike cost line.

Do strikes on AI projects have odds that vanish near parity? That matters for whether strikes pay at the slowest speeds. The answer also depends on the strike cost and on how the gains from a strike change as the leader’s edge grows. It is an empirical conjecture that nothing today settles.

Part 8. Near a ceiling, converging capability can sharpen the motive to strike

Capability that levels off can turn the leader into Powell’s declining state. Suppose capability approaches a ceiling, and the leader’s share changes smoothly near parity with half at parity. Then late in the path the ratio approaches one. With a constant chance of success and free choice of timing, every late enough arrival brings a strike if the cost is below half the chance of success. In the start-only comparison checked by the program, the leader multiplies half the chance of success by the weight it puts on the future after the window.

Now look at the window itself. Hold the strike’s odds and cost fixed across arrival dates, on a path that never passes the ceiling (which holds when capability never falls). At arrival, the follower has at least threshold capability and the leader at most the ceiling. So the largest possible capability ratio is the ceiling measured as a multiple of the threshold. If the threshold lies close enough below the ceiling, the follower arrives near parity, and any strike costing less than half its chance of success pays.

If the odds instead depend on the edge and change smoothly near parity, I prove on paper a parallel result. Near the ceiling a strike comes when the cost is below half the parity odds, and peace holds when it is above. So odds of zero at parity, with any positive cost, remove the strike, though not the motive.

If the threshold lies well below the ceiling, the arrival ratio may still be large, and this result says nothing about the window, because shares lock in at arrival. If shares instead tracked the current ratio, the leader’s share would drift toward half as the ratio approached one. Whether a strike would then pay depends on timing and discounting after arrival that the model does not specify, so that is a conjecture.

Like the band result, this one rests on the jump in the follower’s locked-in share at the threshold. If that share instead rose smoothly with capability, leveling off would shrink each period’s shift toward zero while a positive strike cost stayed fixed. I conjecture that Powell’s condition for war would then eventually fail. The benchmark convergence documented in The War Baseline points toward diminishing returns. Near a ceiling just above the threshold, such convergence sharpens the window problem rather than dissolving it.

Part 9. Several followers and copies can make suppressing everyone cost more than sharing

Several close followers change the leader’s sums. Suppose a number of near followers arrive together after the same lag. Each strike costs the same fixed amount per target and always succeeds, and the survivors split the prize in proportion to their contest strength. Under these conditions I show that suppressing only some followers is strictly worse than the better of suppressing none and suppressing all. When the leader can choose its moment, suppressing everyone is at least as good as peace at or below a cost threshold, and strictly better below it; that threshold falls with each added follower. The per-target cutoff equals the share that any one follower would receive under peace, when the prize is split according to each machine’s contest strength. At parity, suppressing everyone pays only if each strike costs no more than an equal split of the prize among all the machines.

Copies lower that threshold further when each copy adds either a comparable claimant or a redundant holder of a follower’s weights. By the test in When Is a Machine an Actor?, copies count as one actor when their choices, taken together, compare every pair of options, allow ties, and never imply a cycle of preferences. The separate-claimant case needs each holder to bring comparable contest strength. The redundant-holder case applies when the extra holders together keep a single claim alive. Both calculations assume every strike succeeds. Low odds per target are a separate matter.

These results need followers that arrive together, equal follower strength, sure strikes and costs that add up per target. When arrivals are staggered, a Tullock-share example in the technical paper shows that suppressing only some followers can be strictly best when a new entrant reopens the contest. A widely held copy may also be harder to suppress. I do not work out the case of uncertain strikes on several targets. It depends on whether strike outcomes move together and whether failed strikes can be repeated.

Bostrom’s case for the singleton rests on a decisive advantage; I add that being able to suppress any one follower is not enough when suppressing them all costs more than sharing. Yudkowsky and Soares’s scenario shows a related limit when some targets cannot be hit at all: their machine “cannot slow down all the AI labs,” because some datacenters are air-gapped, and a surviving military laboratory’s machine “would demand half the winnings,” so their machine moves against humanity instead (Yudkowsky and Soares 2025).

Part 10. In a later, steeper transition, I conjecture, the roles reverse

Bostrom’s fourth judgment has the same structure seen from the other side. Suppose every machine follows the same growth law in a second transition. By the results of Part 3, a machine that starts that transition earlier gains a decisive capability lead if the growth factor rises without limit, or settles high enough relative to the lag. That late lead can end the world of several machines only if their shares adjust as the capability ratio between them changes. A breakthrough that only one machine can make is not covered by my model.

Before that lead arrives, the roles in the commitment problem reverse. The machine starting the second transition is now the rising side, and the established machines are the declining side whose shares stand to shrink. I conjecture that in this earlier window, the established machines have the motive to strike first. There are two qualifications. An already-arrived initiator holds resources it could credibly hand over, up to its share of what flows during the window. And it faces several peers, who may each hope another will bear the cost of a strike. Once the initiator crosses the new threshold first under a shared growth law, the original window logic gives it a motive to strike lagging peers that are still close enough to contest the prize.

A human proposal for a deterrence regime, in which threats of preventive sabotage check destabilizing AI projects or bids for sole dominance, expresses that declining-side motive as strategy (Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang 2025). Whether a second transition would bring a shift large and fast enough to trigger preventive action remains open. So does whether established machines could see it coming, coordinate and strike in time.

Part 11. Speed, secrecy and open weights: links I conjecture to two earlier papers

Running Through the Rain and Running Toward the Clinic, my papers on speed and risk in the AI cyber transition and on speed, biological risk and health, ask whether a faster approach to superintelligence would be welcome. In the first model, speed means the pace of advance on the way to superintelligence. Here it is the rate of self-improvement once it begins. Both models, though, turn on one clock measured against another. Each of the three links below is my conjecture unless I mark it as proved.

Secrecy may lengthen the lag. In that model a developer temporarily withholds a new capability from general release, sharing it with defenders until catch-up, a rival release, a leak or theft ends its exclusive hold. Followers may need a withheld capability or recipe to begin self-improving, through distillation or copied weights. If so, withholding it lengthens their lag, and by the pace test a longer lag pushes toward one machine. The pace test is proved; the step from secrecy to lag is a conjecture. I conjecture three limits on it:

  • rivals with their own research paths may not be slowed;
  • exclusive rewards for winning can make racing harder, and I do not settle whether harder racing lengthens or shortens lags;
  • secrecy cuts both ways for strikes. It hides the follower progress a leader needs to time a strike, but hidden investment can itself provoke preventive attacks (Debs and Monteiro 2014).

When a faster takeoff might raise long-term risk. The model in Running Through the Rain assumes that long-term risk at superintelligence rises with the pace of advance toward it. The takeoff model does not make the number of machines fall steadily with speed in general. Under the fixed-strike conditions of Part 7, with the leader getting half at parity and its share changing smoothly there, the expected number of machines can follow a rise-and-fall pattern. Near parity, a successful strike leaves one machine and a failed strike leaves two, so the average depends on the chance of success. The count rises to two in the peaceful band, then falls to one where the edge is decisive. That rise-and-fall happens if and only if a strike at parity pays and some speed leaves two machines without a strike. If the peaceful band is empty, the same mix of successes leaving one machine and failures leaving two determines the average at every speed below the decisive edge.

Under those conditions, if there is a positive speed at which two machines emerge without a strike, the same holds at every faster speed that stays strictly below the pace-test rate. At that rate and above it, the leader’s edge is decisive. So near the pace-test rate, a faster takeoff moves the world from two machines to one. If one machine is worse for humans than two, long-term risk rises with speed in that range. That last step is a conjecture, which also assumes that the speed before takeoff and the speed of self-improvement move together.

Open weights cut both ways. Several laboratories, national champions and released weights shorten lags and favor several machines. But releasing weights also widens access to dangerous capabilities. Running Through the Rain draws the needed distinction. An open-weight copy, or a closed copy whose safeguards fail, ends both the exclusion of malicious users and the exclusivity of the leader’s commercial lead. A safeguarded closed copy ends the exclusivity of the lead while continuing to exclude malicious users. If commercial lead plays the part of the lag, safeguarded closed rivals shorten lags without arming attackers, while open weights do both. In Running Toward the Clinic, misuse risk is set by the capability reached or the speed of advance, not the number of holders. Linking open weights to that risk needs an added conjecture: that misuse risk rises with the number of holders.

Part 12. Emergence is only the doorway to a world of several machines

Many Machines, another paper of this series, starts with two machines already in the world. That model says nothing about how machines come to be near-equal or stay so. I supply that entry step here. Those emergence conditions matter for what the two machines do next and for the promises studied in Satiation Is Not Enough.

First, emergence is the gate. Those scenarios apply only where the emergence model leaves at least two machines. That needs an arrival ratio below the decisive multiple, and either peace or a failed strike. It can happen in three settings:

  • inside the band of Part 7, under steady growth with strike odds and costs that do not depend on speed;
  • across the two separate stretches when strike odds vanish at parity as in Part 7’s example;
  • under slower-than-steady growth or a ceiling, where leads fade.

When the growth factor rises without limit, the leader’s capability ratio eventually passes the decisive multiple, so coexistence at arrival requires the follower to cross the threshold before that happens. Where one machine dominates or suppresses its rivals, the world has one machine, the setting of The War Baseline and Satiation Is Not Enough.

Even with a second machine, Many Machines reports that two rivals protect more human-controlled resources than a united machine bloc would only under certain conditions. One is that neither rival is hopeless in a costly war with the other. It also reports that balancing against a would-be dominant machine restrains it only while the others can still beat or deter it, which matches the decisive multiple of Part 2. I conjecture that a second machine can survive below the decisive multiple and still be too weak to meet those conditions for protecting human-controlled resources.

Second, copies bear on surviving the window and on deterrence after arrival. In the same model, mutual deterrence starts from the assumption that each machine can withstand a first strike and hit back because it has backup copies or its model weights are spread out. In my window model, Part 9’s setting at parity gives a related result: with a positive cost per target, enough holders make suppressing everyone worse than peace under either reading of copies. If each holder makes a separate claim, the per-target cutoff is an equal share of the prize among the leader and all the follower-side holders. If the same number of holders instead sustains each follower’s single claim, split the prize equally among the leader and the joint claims, then split a joint claim equally among its holders. That last amount is the per-target cutoff. Without copies, the leader does not necessarily strike; that still turns on the strike condition of Part 6. I conjecture that surviving suppression during the window can help a machine retain the ability to hit back after an attack once it has arrived.

Third, diminishing returns feed both convergence and the preventive motive. Many Machines reports that its bloc rests on machines converging in what they want. Diminishing returns here make machines converge in capability, which is a different thing. The War Baseline reports narrowing benchmark gaps before takeoff as evidence relevant to whether machines converge in what they want. By Part 8, under its conditions, a follower that arrives just below a ceiling arrives near parity, and any strike costing less than half its chance of success pays. Leveling off leaves two arrived machines if the leader chooses peace or its strike fails. That shift in guaranteed shares behind the strike motive comes from the jump at the threshold. And if strike odds rise from zero at parity, a nearly equal follower is also the hardest to stop.

Both models leave open how humans would act as players during the window. Whether humans would help a leader suppress a follower, or shelter the follower, is an open conjecture.

Under the conditions in Satiation Is Not Enough, a machine whose goals are already fully met can credibly promise to stop expanding the resources it controls if further resources would never make it safer. The promise loses credibility where domination would make it safest and fighting is cheap enough. I conjecture that during the window, such a leader loses less from a follower’s arrival only if an arrived rival is no threat. After arrival, mutual deterrence could allow such promises while shifting conflict toward indirect competition over resources humans control. I use different assumptions about commitment in the three models. Any combined account remains a conjecture until one model brings them together.

Part 13. What I have not shown, and what would change the answer

The results here rest on simplifying assumptions, mechanisms I leave out, and quantities nobody has measured.

What the model assumes

  • Every project starts from the same capability, below the threshold, and follows the same fixed growth law, with everyone seeing everything. That starting capability is above zero, and capability stays positive along the path. The starting capability and the growth rule determine the entire path.
  • The leader’s edge is the capability ratio, not the absolute gap. Under steady compounding at a positive rate, any positive lag creates a gap that grows without limit and eventually becomes decisive.
  • Shares lock in at arrival through a contest that costs nothing to run, and the follower’s share jumps when it crosses the threshold.
  • The follower cannot make a binding promise or hand over resources during the window. In the band result its lag is fixed. The extension lets it commit publicly to a longer lag before the window opens, and counts the cost of the wait.
  • The leader can strike once, with the same odds throughout, and can decide just before the follower enters. Since the gain comes after the window, it can put off the cost by waiting. In the start-only version, the gain is multiplied by the leader’s patience, the weight it gives to the future after arrival.
  • The single band of Part 7 assumes strike odds and costs that do not depend on speed.
  • The several-follower result assumes followers who arrive together (so there is one window), equal follower strength, sure strikes and costs that add up per target.

What is proved, and how

The technical paper keeps the original statements and payoff comparisons checked by the proof-checking program as benchmarks. The newer results for the band and for several followers—where the leader chooses when to strike and shares are split in proportion to contest strength—are proved on paper, as are the other additions. Several companion steps to the checked results are also done by hand:

  • the step from the checked strike inequality and Powell’s condition to the leader’s actual choice in the one-decision game, plus versions where the cost depends on the outcome or a strike does only partial damage;
  • connecting the machine-checked parity statements (written directly at zero growth) to the limit of very slow positive growth, which needs the leader’s share to change smoothly near parity;
  • the ceiling result with odds that depend on the edge;
  • the behaviour of the ratio in smooth time, alongside the checked step-by-step version.

The tables and numerical examples are computed, not machine-checked. Containment, shares that grow smoothly before arrival, and the payoffs from uncertain strikes on several followers remain open.

What is not modelled

Different growth laws cut both ways. A follower that improves faster, catches up by benefiting from another project’s advances, or starts higher through distillation, theft or released weights faces a shorter effective lag. A holder of the leader’s own weights has zero lag if it counts as a separate machine. All of this favors several machines on capability.

Conversely, suppose under steady growth at positive rates that the leader grows slightly faster than the follower. Then the arrival ratio grows the farther away the threshold lies. For example, a 10% edge in growth rate, with the threshold ten doublings above the starting point, adds one doubling of effective lag. With any faster-growing leader, the ratio at arrival rises without limit as the threshold lies farther away, and eventually passes any decisive multiple. The ratio is decisive at arrival only if the follower reaches the threshold late enough. If the ratio passes the decisive multiple later, that can change who holds the prize only if shares follow the current ratio. At any fixed arrival date, the ratio changes smoothly with the gap in growth rates. I work this out by hand; it is not machine-checked.

I also leave open several things:

  • a breakthrough that only one machine can make;
  • promises the follower might make during the window;
  • repeated strikes;
  • strike odds that change during the window.

A strike that only delays the follower, rather than removing it, can shift the strike danger away from the slowest takeoffs. If the leader gives the future full weight and the eventual share stays the same, a finite delay by itself brings no bargaining gain.

Further open questions are containment, humanity as a player during the window, and sabotage before any system reaches the threshold, which could change lags and the set of projects. In Disagreement Without Hidden Information, another paper of this series, I treat private information as a separate cause of war, and I set it aside here. A leader that cannot see a rival’s progress cannot time a strike cleanly, though hidden capability can itself provoke preventive conflict. The staggered example of Part 9 shows how unequal arrival dates and unequal strengths together can make partial suppression best.

What nobody has measured, and what would move the answer

No current data settle the key quantities: where the growth factor of self-improvement heads, how long lags between projects will be once self-improvement starts, and how costly, fast and sure strikes on rival AI projects would be, including whether their odds vanish near parity. The narrowing gap between the top model and the tenth, and the three-month open-weight lag reported in The War Baseline, measure benchmarks before any self-improvement.

Three kinds of evidence would move the answer:

  • Toward a single machine on capability: returns that rise without limit, or long lags against short doubling times.
  • Toward a single winner by preventive strike: capability leveling off near the threshold, together with cheap and reliable strikes at parity.
  • Toward several superintelligences: returns that stay bounded or grow slower than steady, short lags across several laboratories or spread-out copies, and strikes that are costly or fail against a near-equal.

Part 14. What to take away

Whether self-improvement produces one superintelligence or several turns on conditions that today’s evidence does not settle. In my model, with advantage measured as a ratio and identical growth laws, it turns on the leader’s edge at the moment the follower crosses the threshold. It also turns on whether stopping near followers and copies in the window costs less than sharing. Under steady compounding, the edge depends on whether doubling is fast compared with the nearest follower’s lag. More projects can bring a closer rival, and released weights can shorten the lag. I leave catch-up through imitation outside the model. With an absolute-gap measure and steady compounding at a positive rate, every positive lag eventually gives the leader a decisive capability edge. Under steady growth with a faster-growing leader, every positive lag is decisive at arrival once the threshold is reached late enough. Bostrom’s own analysis allows several machines when takeoff is slow compared with project lags.

Room on capability is not arrival. Given the jump in the follower’s share at the threshold, the conditions that keep a follower close, a slow takeoff or leveling off near the threshold, can also sharpen the leader’s motive to strike. Whether striking pays also depends on the cost relative to the whole prize, the chance of success against a near-equal, and the number of followers and copy holders under the conditions of Part 9. A failed strike can still leave two machines, and a delay may leave a near rival. A slow takeoff allows several outcomes.

Even if several superintelligences emerge and survive their windows, that alone does not make humans safe. Safety depends on whether the machines converge or compete, on what humans hold that machines value, and on whether rival machines leave any of them able to promise to stop. A comforting conclusion is not available.

Where to read more

  • The formal models, proofs and computed tables are in the appendix to the technical paper, Takeoff and Emergence.
  • The War Baseline (this series): the commitment problem behind preventive war, applied to AI, and the survey of frontier laboratories, national champions, the three-month open-weight lag and narrowing benchmark gaps.
  • When Is a Machine an Actor? (this series): the test for when copies of a model count as one actor.
  • Disagreement Without Hidden Information (this series): private information as a separate cause of war, set aside here.
  • Running Through the Rain: Speed, Secrecy and Risk in the AI Cyber Transition (this series): the secret race and withheld capabilities, the open-weight distinction, and the premise that risk rises with speed.
  • Running Toward the Clinic: Speed, Biological Risk and Health in the AI Transition (this series): misuse risk set by capability or speed rather than the number of holders.
  • Many Machines (this series): what several machines would do once they exist, and the conditions under which two rivals protect more human-controlled resources than a united machine bloc would.
  • Satiation Is Not Enough (this series): when a machine whose goals are already met can credibly promise to stop expanding.
